articles.title: Cops use tear gas, water cannons as over 4 lakh march across country - France protests in videos
articles.summary: France's interior ministry said nearly 1,000 people had been arrested in nationwide protests on Saturday, with the number likely to rise.
articles.body: France's interior ministry said nearly 1,000 people had been arrested in nationwide protests on Saturday, with the number likely to rise.Violent clashes erupted in Paris as police fired tear gas and used water cannons to disperse demonstrators. More than 400,000 people took to the streets to protest against school underfunding and the rising cost of living, with unrest also reported in several other French cities.The procession brought thousands onto the streets and intensified pressure on French President Emmanuel Macron's government.Visuals from the streets of France showed the immense gathering of thousands of protestors holding banners in their hand to express their stance against the rising cost of living.However, what began as a peaceful procession through the French capital turned violent when thousands of demonstrators reached Porte de Vincennes, on the city's southeastern outskirts. Visuals from the scene showed thick clouds of tear gas filling the streets as mask-clad protesters threw cobblestones and other projectiles at security forces.Police deployed armoured water cannons to push back groups of demonstrators in crowded areas. Separate footage showed shopfronts being looted and windows smashed, raising concerns after widespread rioting damaged more than 3,000 businesses across France the previous week.The Paris prosecutor's office confirmed 64 arrests linked to Saturday's protest. Forty people, including six minors, were held in custody, primarily on suspicion of weapons offences or intending to commit violence and damage property.Unrest spreads across France as 70,000 officers deployedClashes were also reported in Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, Strasbourg and Marseille, where police fired tear gas. Water cannons were used to disperse crowds in Nantes and Nice.The French interior ministry estimated that 410,000 people took part in the demonstrations nationwide, including 110,000 in Paris. The CGT trade union, however, put the national turnout at nearly 800,000.France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez deployed 70,000 police officers and security personnel across France, supported by armoured vehicles and helicopters. The security operation followed the previous week's unrest, when authorities acknowledged that police had lost control of several city centres.Security was tightened around major landmarks in Paris, including the Arc de Triomphe. The Louvre and Orsay museums, along with the Art Basel fair, also closed for the weekend as authorities sought to protect prominent venues from further violence.Students, teachers demand better education facilitiesThe demonstrations began last month after complaints about staff shortages at a high school southeast of Paris. The movement has since expanded, drawing students, teachers and trade unions into a wider campaign against deteriorating public education and mounting financial pressures.Government figures show that public middle and high schools lost 15.4 million teaching hours during the 2024-25 school year because staff absences went unreplaced. As a result, 7.5% of scheduled class time was not delivered.Students are demanding 250,000 additional higher education places, changes to the Parcoursup university admissions system, a freeze on rents in public student accommodation and a monthly increase of 200 euros in grants.Economic concerns have added to the discontent. Energy prices rose 21.3% year-on-year in September, while overall inflation reached 3.1%, putting further pressure on households already struggling with the cost of living.Protesters voice anger over inequality and lack of opportunitiesThe march brought together people from different generations and professions, many of whom said they feared the long-term consequences of inadequate public services and rising economic inequality.Camille Chesnier, 27, who has an engineering degree and a master's degree but remains unemployed, described the difficulties faced by young people trying to find work and secure housing."There are enormous numbers of people in the same situation as me but who aren't privileged and who find themselves living on the streets and in squats and, frankly, it's very tough."Bénédicte Pittion, a 46-year-old teacher who marched alongside her 16-year-old daughter, Garance, said the young demonstrators had not received an adequate response from the authorities."The young people who have been demonstrating have not been heard, and as a parent and as a teacher, I stand with them."Garance said she felt "really scared" after the violence during previous weekend protests. However, she argued that staying home would allow the government to claim victory.Soumaya Abed, 58, a veteran nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, criticised the decision to push the march towards the outskirts of Paris."They are using what happened last week as an excuse to quiet protesters. But it won't stop the movement. It won't stop students from demanding better conditions in schools."Louis Ledoux-Xatard, another Paris protester, said growing economic inequality had left him concerned about the country's future."Looking at countries like the United States, we don't want to end up like them, where part of the population has everything and the others have nothing. I never imagined that I'd be taking to the streets so much before my thirties."Macron faces mounting pressure as protesters reject concessionsThe protests pose a fresh challenge to Macron, whose approval ratings have fallen to their lowest levels since he took office in 2017. The unrest comes in the closing months of his term, as discontent over public services and living costs continues to grow.Macron met student representatives on Friday and promised changes to university admissions. However, protest organisers rejected the offer as insufficient, signalling that the government's response has done little to ease tensions.The movement has also drawn comparisons with the yellow vest protests, which began in 2018 over fuel taxes and expanded into a broader revolt against the cost of living and perceived economic inequality.The yellow vest movement has called for another national day of action on October 31 to defend the right to demonstrate, suggesting that the latest clashes may be part of a wider period of unrest rather than an isolated outburst.You use AI every day. articles.title: A New York mortgage lender waited until 2021 to seek a default ruling in a case where a defendant failed to answer in 2018; an October 22 appeals court upheld dismissal of the foreclosure case
articles.summary: A New York appeals court has upheld the dismissal of a mortgage foreclosure lawsuit after the lender waited three years to seek a default judgment against
articles.body: A New York appeals court has upheld the dismissal of a mortgage foreclosure lawsuit after the lender waited three years to seek a default judgment against a defendant who had not responded. The decision enforces state rules that require lenders to take legal action within set deadlines. The ruling was issued on 22 October 2026 by the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Appellate Division, First Department. The judges upheld a lower court's decision to dismiss the foreclosure case because the lender failed to act within the required time after the borrower first failed to respond. According to court filings published by the Appellate Division, First Department, the property owner did not file a formal answer or appear in court in 2018 after receiving the summons and complaint. Under Section 3215(c) of New York's Civil Practice Law and Rules (CPLR), a plaintiff must begin the process of seeking a default judgment within one year after a defendant fails to respond. If the plaintiff misses this deadline, the court must dismiss the case as abandoned unless the lender can provide a good reason for the delay. In this case, the mortgage lender took no concrete steps to obtain a default judgment until 2021, three years after the legal deadline had passed.Strict enforcement of statutory timelinesIn its appeal, the lender asked the court to reverse the trial court's decision to dismiss the case. It tried to explain why it had waited several years between the defendant's failure to respond in 2018 and its request for a default judgment in 2021. However, the First Department judges ruled that the lender had not provided a reasonable explanation for failing to act within the required 12-month period. The appeals court noted that CPLR 3215(c) is designed to stop lenders and financial institutions from leaving lawsuits unresolved for years while interest and administrative fees continue to build up for homeowners facing financial problems. Under New York law, routine office tasks, informal communications or internal transfers of accounts do not meet the requirement to take active steps toward obtaining a judgment. The court stressed that when a lender has no valid legal reason for the delay, the law requires the case to be dismissed.Abandonment rules protect property titlesThe ruling supports long-standing decisions by New York state courts on cases that have been left inactive. Property law attorneys note that enforcing CPLR 3215(c) helps protect homeowners by clearing old cases from court records and preventing unresolved lawsuits from creating lasting problems for property titles. When a court dismisses a foreclosure case as abandoned under CPLR 3215(c), the lender loses its current attempt to obtain a default judgment through that proceeding. If the six-year deadline for enforcing a mortgage has also expired during the intervening years, the lender may be legally prevented from filing a new lawsuit to collect the debt or enforce the mortgage lien. The First Department's order formally ends the appeal and confirms the complete dismissal of the foreclosure case against the property owner.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: US citizenship application gathering dust: Taiwanese Green Card holder sues Trump administration for making him wait around 18 months
articles.summary: Meng Ju Liu, a Taiwanese Green Card holder living in Ohio and waiting for his US citizenship, has now sued the Trump administration over delays, saying
articles.body: Meng Ju Liu, a Taiwanese Green Card holder living in Ohio and waiting for his US citizenship, has now sued the Trump administration over delays, saying that his application has been gathering dust on an office shelf and he has been waiting for an eternity for his citizenship. Newsweek reported that Liu filed the lawsuit in the US District Court for the Southern District of Ohio on October 15, seeking to compel federal officials to complete the processing of his naturalization application.Liu became a Green Card holder in 2002 and he applied for citizenship in April 2025, the report said.Liu has waited around 18 months for his application to progress and has not been called for a naturalization interview, according to court filings. It alleged that USCIS' published processing time for N-400 applications in Cincinnati was 9 1/2 months for 80 percent of cases to be completed. Liu argued that federal officials have failed to process his application within a reasonable period and have not provided a reason for the delay."My decision to apply for US citizenship is driven by the needs of my food import and export business. I sell rice produced in Kansas state to overseas markets, and I believe becoming a US citizen would help me more effectively represent and promote the quality of American agricultural products," Liu told Newsweek."My work also requires me to travel abroad to evaluate contract manufacturers that produce goods for export to the United States. I believe US citizenship and a U.S. passport would provide me with greater security and peace of mind when traveling internationally."A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told Newsweek on Friday, “United States citizenship is a privilege. It should not be a cakewalk to obtain, and we are certainly not going to give it away. USCIS is working to overhaul the test and the entire process to strive towards maximum adherence with the letter and spirit of the law. Naturalization allows aliens to become fully vested members of American society, with important rights and responsibilities that all citizens should exercise and respect. US citizenship is the most meaningful status the US government can bestow, and we are committed to ensuring the integrity of the naturalization process."Immigration attorney Kevin J Andrews noted that the case came at a time when the Department of Homeland Security claimed that naturalizations are down 75%."USCIS posts a processing time of 9.5 months for 80 percent of N-400s in Cincinnati. In May 2025, the agency told him it would reuse fingerprints already on file and run the same security checks on them. As of May 2, 2026, his case status still read as processing. He asks the court to order the checks finished within 30 days and, if he clears them, naturalization within 30 days after that. The most common result of filing a Mandamus lawsuit is an interview notice. The agency often acts before its answer is due, and the case is dismissed as moot. Courts weigh delay differently from district to district. Eighteen months against a posted 9.5 months definitely checks the box," Andrews said.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: Ukraine and Russia exchanged drone strikes on Saturday, with Ukrainian drones hitting a petrochemical plant and an online retailer's warehouse in Russia's Omsk region, while a Russian attack killed three people and injured at least eight others in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region. The strikes also disrupted power supplies across parts of Crimea and Russian-controlled territories in eastern and southern Ukraine, Russia's Energy Ministry said.Ukraine's defence operations company Fire Point said its drones were used to strike a Russian petrochemical plant and a warehouse belonging to online retailer Ozon in Omsk. articles.title: 135 people arrested across France as police find potential weapons on protestors, official says
articles.summary: France Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez says 135 people were arrested as 70,000 police officers deployed to clamp down on nationwide protests.
articles.body: French authorities have so far arrested 135 people Saturday as nationwide protests resumed, France's Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez told reporters. Most of the arrests were prompted after police officers preemptively searched protesters, Reuters reported. Those taken into custody allegedly had items that could be used as weapons, including fireworks and ball bearings. Nuñez did not specify where the arrests were made. In Paris, where tens of thousands of people are marching, police said they have conducted more than 3,000 checks and arrested 65 people, the BBC reported. "Violent individuals have no place in the marches," the Paris Police Department said in a social media post. "The objective is clear: to prevent troublemakers from joining the procession, and to ensure the safety of the demonstrators." AMERICANS WARNED ABOUT PARIS TRAVEL AFTER VIOLENCE, LOOTING AND TEAR GAS-FILLED STREETS Central Paris resembled a city under lockdown, as shopkeepers boarded up storefronts, museums closed and more than 20 metro stations suspended service. In other cities — including Clermont-Ferrand, Grenoble, Lille and Nice — police have resorted to firing tear gas to break up unruly crowds, Reuters reported. Also in Nice, police used a water cannon to disperse a group of demonstrators who refused to pull back. And in Marseille and Lyon, there have been clashes between police officers and hooded youths. FRANCE’S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT Some 70,000 police officers have been deployed across France to clamp down on agitators and prevent the kind of unrest seen during recent demonstrations, when cars were torched and the city hall building in Limoges was set on fire. Last weekend, more than 2,700 people were arrested during protests that later turned into riots and looting sprees. The nationwide marches were meant to reflect broader dissatisfaction with the French government, with protesters taking to the streets to air a range of different grievances. They were frustrated with teacher shortages and poor conditions at schools, including overcrowded classrooms and dilapidated buildings. articles.body: Air India and Air India Express have extended the suspension of flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam until November 7, while services connecting Jeddah will remain cancelled until October 31, amid escalating tensions in the region.The latest extension comes as other Indian carriers, including IndiGo and Akasa Air, have also curtailed operations to Saudi Arabian cities. The disruptions have affected travellers, including Indian Umrah pilgrims, prompting the Indian consulate in Jeddah to step up assistance for those facing cancellations and difficulties arranging alternative travel.Rebooking, refunds for affected passengers"In view of the prevailing situation in the region, Air India and Air India Express flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam will remain suspended until 7 November 2026, while services to and from Jeddah will remain suspended until 31 October 2026," Air India said in a post on X.Passengers with confirmed bookings issued on or before October 24 can opt for flexible rebooking or a full refund upon cancellation.Air India passengers travelling to or from Riyadh and Dammam on dates up to November 7 can avail a one-time complimentary rebooking to or from any operational Air India station in Saudi Arabia, subject to availability, for travel until November 21. For Jeddah, the corresponding rebooking window runs until November 14 for passengers whose original travel dates fall on or before October 31.Air India Express is offering similar options, including alternative routes through operational stations in Saudi Arabia or Bahrain, subject to availability.IndiGo has extended the cancellation of flights to and from Jeddah, Dammam and Madinah until October 31. Its Riyadh services will also remain suspended until October 31.Akasa Air, meanwhile, has extended the suspension of flights to and from Jeddah until November 10 and Riyadh until November 30.Indian consulate steps up assistanceThe Consulate General of India in Jeddah has activated round-the-clock control rooms in Jeddah and Makkah to assist Indian nationals affected by the disruptions, particularly Umrah pilgrims.Working with Indian community associations and volunteers, the consulate is helping arrange food, essential medicines and other immediate relief. articles.title: Seven medals for Army para athletes in Japan; Subedar Dharmaraj Solairaj retains long jump gold with new Asian record
articles.summary: Indian Army’s Paralympic Node won seven medals at the Asian Para Games in Japan; Subedar Dharmaraj Solairaj retained long jump gold with a 7.15m Asian record.
articles.body: Pune: Athletes from Indian Army’s Paralympic Node (APN) secured seven medals, including a historic gold by Subedar Dharmaraj Solairaj, at Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, which concluded on Saturday. Despite fielding a lean squad of only 10 athletes this time, the contingent successfully matched its previous edition’s medal tally.Solairaj (32) successfully defended his men’s long jump title in the combined T44/T62/T64 event. He set a new Asian record with a spectacular leap of 7.15 metres on Thursday. With this victory, the Tamil Nadu-born athlete, who competes in T64 classification, became the first Army para-athlete to win two gold medals at Asian Para Games.Solairaj’s achievement builds on his steady, inspiring progress since returning to the track following a life-altering injury. Recruited into the Madras Regiment in 2013, he underwent a transtibial amputation in 2018 after serving in a high-altitude area along India’s northern border. Initially fearing he would be permanently confined to a wheelchair, he found renewed purpose after interacting with fellow para-athletes at the Army’s Artificial Limb Centre (ALC).His performance has improved consistently through focused training on his run-up, jumping technique, balance, and physical conditioning. In 2025, he had set a national and continental record of 7.32 metres in the T64 category at Indian Open Para Athletics International Championship in Bengaluru.Another major highlight for the Army contingent was the bronze medal clinched by Paris Paralympics bronze medallist Hokato Sema. The 43-year-old registered a throw of 14.65 metres in the men’s F57 shot put event, demonstrating his elite competitiveness against a much younger field. “Age is a crucial factor in this competition, but Sema has once again proven the old adage that age is just a number,” an official noted.Army officials stated that the seven-medal haul is highly commendable given their reduced representation. Strict entry caps imposed by the organisers prevented the Army from fielding its core para-rowers and athletes in canoeing and kayaking. “We could have won significantly more medals had our rowers and kayakers been permitted to participate,” the official added.The contingent’s performance also brought to light the technical challenges faced by para-athletes, particularly those using running prostheses. Fine-tuning prosthetics and sockets to different competition surfaces and unpredictable weather conditions remains a critical challenge, as even microscopic variations can heavily impact balance, comfort, and final performance.Housed on the campus of Bombay Engineering Group and Centre, APN trains and supports injured soldiers looking to rebuild their lives through competitive sports. Officials noted that Solairaj’s journey—from an injury that threatened to derail his sporting ambitions to successfully defending his continental title—underscores the crucial role of sustained coaching, rehabilitation, and structural physical conditioning.PM appreciates Solairaj’s achievementPrime Minister Narendra Modi took to his official X platform to praise the long jumper’s landmark victory, writing: “Solairaj Dharmaraj has delivered an exceptional performance in the men’s long jump T44/T62/T64 event at Asian Para Games 2026, winning gold with a phenomenal jump. By surpassing his own Asian record, he has once again demonstrated his tremendous skills and determination. Congratulations to Solairaj on this outstanding triumph. articles.title: A bridge in fallen Maoist HQ Abujmarh is new symbol of change in once forbidden zone
articles.summary: Improvised 60m bridge in Abujmarh, built by C-60 commandos and tribals, links Binagunda and boosts access to schools, healthcare in former Maoist hub.
articles.body: Nagpur: An improvised 60metre-long bridge built by C-60 commandos and tribal villagers in the heart of the fallen Maoist headquarters of Abujmarh has emerged as a symbol of the changing ground reality in the once booby-trapped forbidden zone. Straddling a deep ravine where waters swell and maroon the picturesque Binagonda for six months during the monsoon, the bridge is a lifeline for villagers, particularly schoolchildren, pregnant mothers and critically ill patients.The bridge was constructed on a war footing in the dense forests by bundling mammoth cement pipes with cranes and then deploying tractors and bulldozers to smoothen tonnes of gravel and ‘murrum’ to fortify the structure. Binaguna was a strategic point in the Red Corridor — impregnable for four decades.Despite its breathtaking natural beauty that earned Binagunda the epithet of ‘Kashmir of Vidarbha’, the region was in the blind spot of development. The change gathered momentum following the March 31 deadline set by Union home minister Amit Shah to eliminate Left-Wing Extremism. With the Maoist network smashed, civic infrastructure is expanding into these remote areas.On October 22, security personnel from Binagunda police assistance centre, Central Reserve Police Force, State Reserve Police Force and elite C-60 commandos joined hands with villagers to construct the bridge.Pregnant women, senior citizens and patients requiring urgent medical attention will benefit from improved access to healthcare. articles.title: AIIMS-Nagpur gets ₹30cr NCDC sanction for BSL-III lab to strengthen infectious disease surveillance, research
articles.summary: AIIMS Nagpur gets ₹30 crore NCDC sanction for BSL-III lab to boost high-risk infectious disease detection, surveillance and research; operational in ~1 year.
articles.body: Nagpur: AIIMS-Nagpur has received a Rs30 crore sanction from National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), New Delhi, to establish a Biosafety Level-III (BSL-III) laboratory, a facility expected to strengthen the region’s capacity to detect and investigate emerging and high-risk infectious diseases.The laboratory is expected to become operational in about a year. “Space had already been earmarked for the facility and the sanctioned amount would be used for developing its infrastructure,” AIIMS executive director Prashant Joshi said. Manpower and equipment would be funded through separate budgets.Joshi added that the facility will reduce dependence on National Institute of Virology (NIV), Pune, for advanced testing and help strengthen Maharashtra’s capacity for infectious disease surveillance and research.The development comes at a time when increasing human-animal interaction, deforestation and climate change are creating conditions for the emergence and spread of zoonotic infections. “Human-animal interface is increasing because of deforestation. We are invading the habitat of animals. Climate change and deforestation are very important factors,” said Joshi.Meena Mishra, head of the department of microbiology, AIIMS-Nagpur, said early detection of emerging infections required both syndromic and genomic surveillance. While syndromic surveillance identifies unusual patterns of illness based on symptoms, genomic surveillance helps detect mutations and emerging pathogens through whole genome sequencing.“If the incidence of a disease is increasing, it should be picked up through proper syndromic surveillance as well as genomics at an early stage so that proper preventive measures can be implemented,” Mishra said.In another major upgrade, AIIMS Nagpur’s Virus Research and Diagnostic Laboratory (VRDL) is being converted into an Infectious Disease Research and Diagnostic Laboratory (IRDL) at a cost of Rs17 crore. The project is being funded by ICMR-DHR. The upgraded regional facility will cover bacteriology, mycology, parasitology and virology, besides expanding the range of infections that can be tested. Subsequent raids across Delhi-NCR led to the arrest of the accused.Police said Khan had previously worked as a salesman in a wholesale garment market and was familiar with the business practices of traders. Investigators alleged that he had incurred heavy losses in cricket betting and resorted to cheating to repay debts.Police said the accused disclosed that he had sold the medical equipment to a firm in Delhi at a fraction of its value. articles.title: No scam, textbooks bought at lower rates, claims Sood; AAP wants penalty for supply delay
articles.summary: Delhi textbook procurement row: Minister Ashish Sood denies scam, says Class VIII Hindi book bought for Rs 28.60; AAP seeks penalty for supply delays.
articles.body: New Delhi: A day after AAP alleged irregularities in Delhi govt’s procurement of school textbooks, education minister Ashish Sood Saturday rejected the charges, claiming that govt had bought a Class-VIII Hindi textbook for Rs 28.60 against the Rs 65 book cited by AAP.He also accused the opposition party of misleading the public by making allegations without verifying procurement rates and tender specifications, describing the allegations as an example of what he called its “hoot and shoot” politics.One of the principal allegations concerned the procurement of Malhar, the Class-VIII Hindi textbook. AAP had questioned govt’s purchase price in comparison with the prices at which the book was available from National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT).Sood said Delhi govt had procured Malhar for Rs 28.60 per copy, substantially below the Rs 65 book cited by AAP. He further claimed that under the previous AAP govt in 2022, a Griha Vigyan textbook of comparable dimensions was printed for Rs 55 per copy.The minister also referred to two letters dated Aug 17 and Sept 6, 2023, and issued by the then education secretary, which, Sood said, raised concerns about the quality of printing and textbooks supplied during the previous govt’s tenure. He claimed that these records contradicted AAP’s criticism of the current procurement process.Responding to the allegations concerning their dimensions, Sood cited the tender specifications, which prescribed a size of 17.1cm x 24.1cm (A4/standard format). He maintained that the dimensions were consistent with those followed in previous years and could be measured using scales, which were distributed at his news conference.Sood also explained that NCERT had increased the size of its textbooks this year, but the tender for the current academic year was issued last year, when the earlier specifications were in place.Responding to allegations of 40% commission, Sood said, “Tell lies, make false claims of 40% commission, and run away. They don’t even know the price of a single book, yet they claim a scam.” He claimed that a “60% commission business” ran during AAP’s tenure, “which would be exposed soon”.Refuting AAP’s claim of higher textbook costs, the minister claimed that textbook prices had declined across several classes, despite inflation. articles.title: A Bee Gees song released in 1979 still generates money for children; royalties from ‘Too Much Heaven’ have contributed to more than $10 million in UNICEF funding
articles.summary: A song released by the Bee Gees in 1979 continues to support children around the world, decades after it first reached audiences.
articles.body: A song released by the Bee Gees in 1979 continues to support children around the world, decades after it first reached audiences. ‘Too Much Heaven’ became part of a fundraising initiative that allowed the band to donate royalties to the United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF). The arrangement has generated more than $10 million in contributions, helping sustain programmes that improve children’s lives. According to UNICEF, the money has become part of a wider pool of funding supporting long-term projects, including access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene education in vulnerable communities.How does the Bee Gees song continue to support childrenThe story of Too Much Heaven began with a decision to use music for a purpose beyond entertainment. In 1979, the Bee Gees performed the song at the Music for UNICEF Concert, dedicating its royalties to programmes for children worldwide.According to UNICEF, the contribution has raised more than $10 million in flexible, non-restricted funding. This means the money can support different areas of UNICEF’s work rather than being limited to one particular project.The arrangement also means the song continues to generate funds whenever it is played. The 1979 concert marked an important moment in the relationship between the music industry and charitable giving. By donating royalties from popular songs, musicians created a way for their work to keep contributing to children's welfare long after its original release.The 1979 concert brought leading musicians togetherThe Music for UNICEF: Gift of Song concert took place at the United Nations General Assembly in 1979. It was organised by the Bee Gees, their manager Robert Stigwood and British television host David Frost.The event brought together several prominent performers, including ABBA, Donna Summer, Earth, Wind & Fire, Rod Stewart, Olivia Newton-John, Kris Kristofferson and Rita Coolidge.The artists pledged royalties from their songs to UNICEF. Among the tracks included in the initiative were ABBA’s Chiquitita, Rod Stewart’s Do Ya Think I’m Sexy? and the Bee Gees’ Too Much Heaven.The commitment was significant because it extended beyond a single fundraising performance. Instead of limiting their support to money raised on the night, the musicians agreed to donate income generated by their music over time.UNICEF’s account records Barry Gibb, the Bee Gees’ chief songwriter, explaining that the group wanted to give something back after earning substantial money. His brother Robin Gibb also recognised the urgent needs of children, particularly in areas such as food, medicine and education.Why do music royalties make a lasting differenceTraditional fundraising events often depend on donations collected at a particular time. Royalties from music offer another approach because a song can continue generating income through repeated listening and purchases.According to UNICEF, donated songs can produce funds whenever they are streamed, purchased or played. This creates an ongoing source of support rather than a contribution tied to a single event. Too Much Heaven illustrates how that model can work across generations. Although the song was released in 1979, its contribution has continued into the present day.The money is also flexible, allowing UNICEF to direct resources towards different needs as circumstances change. This is particularly important for an organisation working across countries and communities where access to basic services remains uneven.UNICEF’s history of music and giving also highlights the contributions of artists such as George Harrison, Ravi Shankar, Fleetwood Mac and ABBA.A village in India shows how long-term funding can helpThe impact of sustained support becomes clearer through the experience of Bandaguda, a village in Odisha, India, described in UNICEF’s March 2026 article about the Bee Gees’ contribution.The community once faced serious challenges in accessing safe drinking water and sanitation. Residents relied on streams for everyday needs, while inadequate sanitation exposed families to waterborne illnesses.Naranga, a village resident, experienced the consequences personally when her youngest child died from diarrhoea. The loss became a turning point, prompting her to work with other women to improve sanitation and hygiene in the community.UNICEF had been working with government partners since the early 1980s to expand access to safe water and strengthen health monitoring. Funding from various sources, including the broader pool of contributions supported by the Bee Gees’ song royalties, has helped sustain UNICEF programmes. The money is not presented as the sole reason for the village’s progress, but as part of the wider support that enables communities to build lasting improvements.By 2011, Bandaguda had become the first tribal village in Odisha to be declared open defecation free, according to UNICEF.Women are building on the progress made by earlier generationsThe changes in Bandaguda have continued beyond the initial improvements in sanitation. Women who once struggled to access basic services have become community leaders, helping families adopt healthier practices and encouraging wider participation in local development.UNICEF reports that the district government selected Self-Help Groups to promote sanitation across the region in 2015. Women involved in these groups helped households understand the importance of toilets and hygiene, while community initiatives made construction more affordable.The results have influenced younger generations. Kalpana, Naranga’s daughter, now conducts menstrual health training for adolescent girls and helps teach young children proper handwashing techniques.According to UNICEF, access to piped safe drinking water in Koraput district rose from less than 3% in 2019 to more than 68% in 2026. Schools in the area also have toilets and handwashing facilities, allowing children to practise hygiene as part of their daily routines. articles.summary: An Indian woman who travelled to Australia to care for her seriously ill brother says she will have to return to India with his estate still unsettled
articles.body: An Indian woman who travelled to Australia to care for her seriously ill brother says she will have to return to India with his estate still unsettled after Australian authorities rejected her request for more time to stay in the country, ABC News Australia reported.Shipra Saini moved to Australia in 2025 to look after her brother, who died from a brain haemorrhage on November 1 last year. She is now living in Ballarat, Victoria, trying to manage his affairs, including obtaining a death certificate and probate, selling his home and belongings, transferring possessions to India, paying expenses and distributing the remaining assets.Saini estimated she spent more than $40,000 on visa applications, living costs and settling the estate. Restrictions on her ability to work have forced her to rely on a loan."Until my brother was here, [Australia] was a beautiful country," she said, adding that the visa process had made her feel she had "lost the charm of this country".In August 2026, Saini sought another visa after her solicitor advised that she needed at least six more months. Her application was rejected, and her existing visa, carrying condition 8503, expires on October 30.The condition generally prevents holders from applying for most other visas within Australia without a waiver. Saini said delays in obtaining probate and selling the property were beyond her control. Under pressure to meet the deadline, she accepted the first offer for her brother's home instead of waiting for a potentially better one."I'm on the brink of breaking down," she said, describing the situation as an additional burden while grieving her brother.Saini says she will go back to India, will settle issues remotelySaini plans to return to India later this month. She will miss her brother's November memorial service and will be unable to attend the property settlement or complete his employment-related entitlements, including superannuation, in person with her solicitor's help.The Department of Home Affairs said it could not comment on individual cases for privacy reasons.Immigration lawyer Jordan Tew said the system needed greater "flexibility" for people facing compassionate circumstances. He argued that administering a deceased relative's estate was different from seeking additional time for leisure or work, and that selling property could take longer than expected.Tew warned that the government's plan to extend condition 8503 to all visitor visas could leave more people needing waivers when their circumstances change. He said the concern was not migration targets themselves, but how policies were implemented and whether genuine applicants were caught up in restrictions.Saini said her experience illustrated the human cost of the political focus on reducing migration."How could they be treating the immigrants this way?" she asked."Politicians, they just go with the wave of whatever is going on," she said, arguing that the political climate had made people less willing to help.You use AI every day.
